stemBlocks.value: The diagram shows the vectors a and b drawn from the origin O on a coordinate grid, with a reaching the point (3, 2) and b reaching the point (−3, 3). (a) Write a and b as column vectors.
Think first: Read each arrow as 'how far across, then how far up' from the origin to the arrowhead.

stemBlocks.altText: Source visual for edmar-csec-p180-q06 from workbook page 180.

solutionSteps.instruction: Follow the arrow labelled a from O.

contentBlocks.value: It runs 3 units to the right and 2 units up, ending at (3, 2)

solutionSteps.instruction: Follow the arrow labelled b from O.

contentBlocks.value: It runs 3 units to the left and 3 units up, ending at (−3, 3)
Right and up are positive; left and down are negative, so the horizontal component of b is negative
Top entry is the horizontal step, bottom entry is the vertical step

strategyBlocks.value: Follow each arrow from O to its tip, counting the horizontal steps first and then the vertical steps, keeping left and down negative.

finalAnswerBlocks.value: (a) a is the column vector with components 3 and 2; b is the column vector with components −3 and 3.

whyThisWorks.value: A vector drawn from the origin has components identical to the coordinates of its endpoint, because both describe the same journey out from O. The order in a column vector is fixed — horizontal on top, vertical below — and the signs record direction, so a leftward step is a negative first component. Getting the sign right is what distinguishes b from the vector (3, 3).

commonErrors.misconception: Writing b as (3, 3) and losing the negative sign for the leftward movement.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Writing b as (3, 3) and losing the negative sign for the leftward movement.

commonErrors.misconception: Reversing the order and writing (2, 3) for a.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Reversing the order and writing (2, 3) for a.

commonErrors.misconception: Counting the fine sub-gridlines instead of the labelled units.

examTip.value: Check which labelled gridline the arrowhead sits on before writing components — fine sub-gridlines are the usual cause of an off-by-one reading.
